title: Great Is Your Faithfulness
summary: A single man who has felt God's hand against him describes his affliction in stark images: darkness, chains, a prayer shut out, arrows in his body. Then, in the middle of his despair, he calls to mind the LORD's loving devotion and mercies, which are new every morning, and resolves to wait for God. He calls the people to examine their ways and return to the LORD, laments again, and ends by recalling that God heard him from the pit and asking God to judge his enemies.
story: Chapters 1 and 2 spoke of the city; chapter 3 narrows to one person. The speaker calls himself the man who has seen affliction. He may be an individual such as Jeremiah, who was lowered into a cistern (Jeremiah 38:6) as this man is dropped into a pit (verse 53), or he may be an everyman figure standing for the whole people. Either way, the national catastrophe is now felt in one body. This is also the book's center, both in position and in meaning. It is here that hope first appears, and it appears not after the suffering ends but in the middle of it. The chapter shows the movement the whole book is reaching for: from despair, through remembering who God is, to repentance and prayer.
historical:
The chapter belongs to the aftermath of Jerusalem's fall to Babylon in 587 or 586 BC, though it contains fewer specific historical details than the other poems. The references to being a laughingstock to his own people (verse 14), to enemies who hunted him (verse 52), and to being thrown into a pit with stones cast on him (verse 53) could fit the experience of a prophet like Jeremiah, who was mocked, imprisoned, and left in a muddy cistern during the siege (Jeremiah 20:7; 37 and 38). They could also be the traditional images of the psalms of lament, where the pit and deep waters stand for the threat of death (Psalms 69 and 88).

The communal section (verses 40 to 47) speaks for the survivors as a group: scum and refuse among the nations, surrounded by enemies. That matches the situation of Judah after the fall, when its people lived under Babylonian rule at home and as deportees abroad, mocked by neighbors who had once feared them.
cultural:
Many of the chapter's images come from Israel's everyday life. The rod of wrath (verse 1) is the shepherd's or parent's rod of discipline. The yoke (verse 27) was the wooden bar on the neck of oxen and a standard picture of subjection or training. Wormwood and gall (verses 15 and 19) were bitter plants, proverbial for anything bitter or poisonous. The prisoners crushed underfoot and the man denied justice in his lawsuit (verses 34 to 36) point to the courts and prisons of the ancient world, where the powerful could easily crush the poor; the poem insists that God sees and does not approve.

The man who says “The LORD is my portion” (verse 24) is using the language of inheritance. When Israel entered the land, each tribe received a portion of territory, except the Levites, whose portion was the LORD himself (Numbers 18:20). To say that God is one's portion, after the land has been lost, is to claim an inheritance that no army can take away.
literary: The chapter is the most elaborate acrostic in the Bible outside Psalm 119. It has sixty-six verses in twenty-two groups of three, and all three verses in each group begin with the same letter of the Hebrew alphabet. The speaker shifts. Verses 1 to 20 are an individual lament in which God is the unnamed He who has done all these things. Verse 21 turns: Yet I call this to mind. Verses 22 to 39 are almost like wisdom teaching, reflecting on God's goodness, the value of waiting, and the justice of God. Verses 40 to 47 become a communal confession and lament (we and us). Verses 48 to 66 return to an individual voice, weeping, then recalling a past deliverance and praying for justice. The central verses, 22 to 24, are the pivot of the whole book. There is a small textual question in verse 22: the standard Hebrew text reads we are not consumed, while some ancient translations read his mercies do not cease; either way the meaning is that God's loving devotion has not come to an end.

outline.t: The man who has seen affliction: God's hand against him
Yet I call this to mind: the LORD's loving devotion
The goodness of waiting and the justice of God
Let us examine our ways and return
Tears that flow until the LORD looks down
God heard from the pit: a prayer for vindication

doctrines.note: The chapter's hope rests entirely on God's character: his loving devotion, his compassion, and his faithfulness (verses 22 and 23). It also insists that “He does not willingly afflict or grieve the sons of men” (verse 33). Suffering is real, but it is not God's heart toward his people.

Hope here is an act of memory and will. After saying his hope has perished (verse 18), the speaker says, “Yet I call this to mind, and therefore I have hope” (verse 21). Hope is not the absence of pain but the decision to fix the mind on what God has revealed of himself.
“Let us examine and test our ways, and turn back to the LORD” (verse 40). The communal section models honest self-examination in the face of disaster, joined with prayer.

The chapter holds together God's sovereignty over all events (verses 37 and 38) and his refusal to delight in affliction. It gives no neat theory, but it gives a way to live: wait quietly, sit in silence, and keep turning toward God.

words.note: Chesed, translated loving devotion (older versions: steadfast love, lovingkindness, mercy). It names loyal, committed love within a covenant, love that keeps its promises when the other party has failed. In verse 22 it is the reason the people are not consumed; in verse 32 it is abundant even when God causes grief.

Rachamim, compassion or mercies. The word is related to the Hebrew for womb, and it carries the sense of a tender, visceral love like a mother's for her child. These mercies, the poem says, never fail and are new every morning.

Emunah, faithfulness, reliability, firmness. It describes someone who can be leaned on without giving way. “Great is Your faithfulness” (verse 23) is the first moment in the chapter when the speaker turns to address God directly, and it is praise. The line gave its name to a much-loved hymn by Thomas Chisholm (1923).

Cheleq, portion or share, especially an inherited plot of land. The speaker's soul says the LORD is his portion (verse 24): having lost land, city, and temple, he claims God himself as his inheritance.

christ: The man who has seen affliction under the rod of God's wrath is not predicted to be the Messiah, but Christian readers have long seen in him a pattern that Jesus fulfills. Jesus was a laughingstock to his own people, mocked in song, given bitter drink, shut in, and handed over to death. Verse 30, “Let him offer his cheek to the one who would strike him,” anticipates his own teaching (Matthew 5:39) and his silence before those who struck him. Most of all, the chapter's central claim, that the LORD's loving devotion never ceases and his mercies are new every morning, is grounded for Christians in the cross and the empty tomb, where God's covenant love was shown to be stronger than death. Where this man felt God's wrath for sin shared with his people, Jesus bore it for them. The link is one of pattern, not prediction, and it is no less real for that.

hard.q: How can a book of Scripture say that God shuts out prayer and tears a person to pieces, and in the same chapter call him good and compassionate?
hard.a: The chapter does not solve this tension; it lives inside it. The first twenty verses describe how affliction feels: God seems to be a bear, a lion, an archer, a jailer, one who refuses to listen. The Bible does not censor that experience. The psalms of lament (for example Psalms 13, 22, and 88) speak the same way, and Job does too. Then the speaker does something deliberate: he calls to mind what he knows of God's character, and that becomes the ground of his hope. Some readers emphasize that the chapter teaches God's sovereign hand in all things, good and adverse (verses 37 and 38). Others emphasize verse 33, that God does not afflict from his heart, and see suffering as permitted within his purposes rather than desired. Both readings agree that the speaker's honesty about his pain is not unbelief, and that hope in the chapter is chosen rather than felt. If this chapter describes where you are right now, darkness without light and prayer that seems to hit a ceiling, you are not the first person of faith to be there, and you don't have to stay there alone. Tell someone you trust, reach out to a pastor, a counselor, or a doctor, and if you are having thoughts of ending your life, call or text 988 (the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline in the United States) or your local emergency number today.

questions: The speaker says his hope has perished and, three verses later, that he has hope. What does he do in between, and what might that look like for you?
“It is good to wait quietly for the salvation of the LORD” (verse 26). Why is waiting quietly so difficult, and what does it require?
Which part of this chapter do you most need right now: the honest lament, the reminder of God's faithfulness, or the call to examine your ways? Why?
